SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology09 / 20
The U.S. Health Care System

Not a system, but a LABYRINTH!

A fee-for-service (FFS) system (market-driven)

Major part in private hands

A patchwork of providers, increasingly consolidated

Fragmented financing and delivery of health care

Multiple providers make their own decisions as to how much to charge of each type of service.

Multiple payers negotiates with the providers regarding how much to pay for each type of service.

Numerous insurance agencies offer various providers multiple mechanisms for insuring against risks.

Numerous consulting firms offer services to both providers and payers in planning, cost containment, quality, and management.

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology10 / 20
Factors Driving Up the Medical Costs

The fee-for-service system (incentives for doing more unnecessary services, and for charging high)

Lack of transparency (uninformed consumers)

Complex system obscure the costs (consumers not motivated to negotiate, the “someone else’s money” phenomenon.)

High transaction costs (because of the complex system, e.g., overheads)

Defensive medicine increases unnecessary services

The monopoly (the myth of a “free” health care market)

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology12 / 20
Medicalization

The transformation of a human condition into a medical matter to be treated by medical professionals.

Involving defining the “sick role”.

A process of social construction

E.g., ADHD, Autism, pregnancy, menopause, obesity, …

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology13 / 20
Sociological Perspectives on Medicalization

Functionalist Perspective

Medicalization is a social control mechanism critical for maintaining social order and functioning

Sickness as “deviance” that needs to be controlled

The function of medicine is to help the society retain order and normal functioning by regulating human body

By preventing and/or treating illnesses

By controlling the assignment of the “sick role” to people

The “Sick Role”

The sick person is exempt from “normal” social roles

The sick person is not responsible for his or her condition

The sick person should try to get well

The sick person should seek technically competent help and cooperate with the physician

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology14 / 20
Sociological Perspectives on Medicalization

Symbolic Interactionist Perspective

Sickness has a social dimension, it is socially constructed (e.g., Gender Identity Disorder, ADHD)

Not everyone sick will be assigned “the sick role” (e.g., children with ADHD in China)

Not everyone assigned the sick role is actually sick

SOC 2010 · Introduction to Sociology15 / 20
Sociological Perspectives on Medicalization

Conflict Perspective

Assignment of a “sick role” and medicalization involve power struggle

It systematically benefits those in power

Example: homosexuality

In 2012, the American Psychiatric Association’s board of trustees approved changes to the latest version of The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders  (DSM-V) that will remove the term “Gender Identity Disorder” (GID) which has historically been used by mental health professionals to diagnose transgender individuals. Simultaneously, the term “Gender Dysphoria” will be used to describe emotional distress over “a marked incongruence between one’s experienced/expressed gender and assigned gender.”
